records.source: וַיְהִ֨י מִיָּמִ֜ים בִּימֵ֣י קְצִיר־חִטִּ֗ים וַיִּפְקֹ֨ד שִׁמְשׁ֤וֹן אֶת־אִשְׁתּוֹ֙ בִּגְדִ֣י עִזִּ֔ים וַיֹּ֕אמֶר אָבֹ֥אָה אֶל־אִשְׁתִּ֖י הֶחָ֑דְרָה וְלֹֽא־נְתָנ֥וֹ אָבִ֖יהָ לָבֽוֹא׃
records.gloss: And it was after days, in [the] days of [the] harvest of wheat, and visited Samson his wife with a kid of goats, and he said, let me go in to my wife into the chamber; and not let him her father go in.
pieces: Some time later, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife, taking a young goat with him. He said, "I am going in to my wife in her room." But her father would not let him go in.

L.1: And it was after [some] days, in the days of the wheat harvest, that Samson visited his wife with a young goat. And he said, "Let me go in to my wife, into the chamber." But her father did not let him go in.

R.1: Some time later, during the wheat harvest, Samson went to see his wife. He took a young goat with him as a gift. He said, "I want to go into my wife's room to be with her." But her father would not let him go in.

decisions.choice: the wheat harvest: late spring, when the grain stood ripe in the fields
decisions.reason: Wheat was harvested in late spring, after the barley. The time is given because the fields were full of standing and cut grain, ready to burn (verse 5).

decisions.choice: visited his wife with a young goat: came to her with a gift
decisions.reason: A young goat was a fitting gift, as when Judah promised one to Tamar (Genesis 38:17). Samson had left in anger after the wedding feast (14:19) and now came back expecting to take up his marriage, not knowing that she had been given to another man (14:20).

decisions.choice: go in to my wife into the chamber: to sleep with her as her husband
decisions.reason: To "go in to" a woman is a common way of speaking of a man coming to his wife to sleep with her (Genesis 29:21; 30:3). The "chamber" is the inner room of the house.

decisions.choice: as a gift; to be with her
decisions.reason: Readable says that the goat was a gift and says plainly what going in to his wife meant, without making the language explicit.

records.heading: Samson burns the Philistines' grain

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אָבִ֗יהָ אָמֹ֤ר אָמַ֨רְתִּי֙ כִּי־שָׂנֹ֣א שְׂנֵאתָ֔הּ וָאֶתְּנֶ֖נָּה לְמֵרֵעֶ֑ךָ הֲלֹ֨א אֲחֹתָ֤הּ הַקְּטַנָּה֙ טוֹבָ֣ה מִמֶּ֔נָּה תְּהִי־נָ֥א לְךָ֖ תַּחְתֶּֽיהָ׃
records.gloss: And said her father, saying I said that hating you hated her, and I gave her to your companion; [is] not her sister the younger better than she? let her be, please, to you instead of her.
pieces: Her father said, "I was sure that you hated her completely, so I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister more beautiful than she is? Please take her instead."

L.2: And her father said, "I truly said [to myself] that you utterly hated her, and I gave her to your companion. Is not her younger sister better than she? Let her be yours, please, instead of her."

R.2: Her father said, "I really thought you hated her, so I gave her to your friend as his wife. But her younger sister is even prettier than she is. Please take her as your wife instead."

decisions.choice: I truly said ... you utterly hated her: he was certain Samson had rejected her
decisions.reason: Both verbs are doubled for emphasis ("saying I said", "hating you hated"). "Said" here means said to himself, that is, thought. The father claims he was sure the marriage was over, since Samson had gone home in anger (14:19).

decisions.choice: your companion: the man who had attended Samson at the wedding
decisions.reason: This is the companion of 14:20, one of the young men who stood with Samson at the feast, the groom's attendant. Giving the bride to him made the insult worse.

decisions.choice: better: more attractive
decisions.reason: The word means "good" in a broad sense; set beside a woman as a bride it speaks of her looks, as in Genesis 24:16 and 26:7.

decisions.choice: more beautiful / prettier; take her instead
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "better" means here, and turn "let her be to you" into the plain offer of marriage it is. Readable states the question as the statement it expects.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָהֶם֙ שִׁמְשׁ֔וֹן נִקֵּ֥יתִי הַפַּ֖עַם מִפְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים כִּֽי־עֹשֶׂ֥ה אֲנִ֛י עִמָּ֖ם רָעָֽה׃
records.gloss: And said to them Samson, I am blameless this time from [the] Philistines when doing I with them harm.
pieces: Samson said to them, "This time no one can blame me when I do the Philistines harm."

L.3: And Samson said to them, "This time I [am] blameless toward the Philistines when I do them harm."

R.3: Samson told them, "This time I have every right to pay the Philistines back. No one can blame me for the harm I am going to do to them."

decisions.choice: blameless: free of guilt, in the right
decisions.reason: The verb means to be clean or free of guilt. Samson claims that what was done to him gives him the right to strike back, so no one can hold it against him.

decisions.choice: this time: unlike the earlier occasion
decisions.reason: "This time" looks back to 14:19, when he killed thirty men of Ashkelon to pay his wager. Now, he says, he has a just cause.

decisions.choice: to them: to the father and the people of the household
decisions.reason: "Them" is plural, though only the father has spoken. Samson's answer is addressed to the household and the Philistines of the town around him.

decisions.choice: I have every right to pay the Philistines back
decisions.reason: Readable spells out what being "blameless" means here in a sentence of its own.

records.source: וַיֵּ֣לֶךְ שִׁמְשׁ֔וֹן וַיִּלְכֹּ֖ד שְׁלֹשׁ־מֵא֣וֹת שׁוּעָלִ֑ים וַיִּקַּ֣ח לַפִּדִ֗ים וַיֶּ֤פֶן זָנָב֙ אֶל־זָנָ֔ב וַיָּ֨שֶׂם לַפִּ֥יד אֶחָ֛ד בֵּין־שְׁנֵ֥י הַזְּנָב֖וֹת בַּתָּֽוֶךְ׃
records.gloss: And went Samson and caught three hundred foxes, and took torches, and turned tail to tail, and put torch one between [the] two the tails in [the] middle.
pieces: So Samson went and caught 300 foxes. He took torches, tied the foxes together in pairs, tail to tail, and set a torch in the middle, between the two tails of every pair.

L.4: And Samson went and caught 300 foxes, and took torches, and turned [them] tail to tail, and put one torch between the two tails, in the middle.

R.4: So Samson went out and caught 300 foxes. He tied them together in pairs by their tails. Then he fastened a torch between the tails of each pair.

decisions.choice: foxes, or possibly jackals
decisions.reason: The word usually means foxes, but it may also include jackals, which live in packs and are easier to catch in large numbers (Psalm 63:11; Lamentations 5:18). The story does not depend on which animal is meant.

decisions.choice: turned tail to tail: joined them in pairs by the tails
decisions.reason: Two animals tied together would pull against each other and run wildly rather than back to their dens, spreading the fire over a wide area.

decisions.choice: tied ... together in pairs
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only that he "turned" them tail to tail; Balanced and Readable say how, since a torch between two tails means the pairs were tied.

records.source: וַיַּבְעֶר־אֵשׁ֙ בַּלַּפִּידִ֔ים וַיְשַׁלַּ֖ח בְּקָמ֣וֹת פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיַּבְעֵ֛ר מִגָּדִ֥ישׁ וְעַד־קָמָ֖ה וְעַד־כֶּ֥רֶם זָֽיִת׃
records.gloss: And he kindled fire in the torches, and he sent [them] into [the] standing grain of [the] Philistines, and he burned from stacked sheaves and to standing grain and to vineyard, olive.
pieces: He set the torches on fire and let the foxes loose in the Philistines' standing grain. He burned up everything, from the stacked sheaves to the uncut grain, and the vineyards and olive groves as well.

L.5: And he set fire to the torches and sent [them] into the standing grain of the Philistines, and he burned [everything] from the stacked sheaves to the standing grain, and to the vineyards [and] olive groves.

R.5: He lit the torches and let the foxes run into the Philistines' fields of ripe grain. The fire burned up the bundles of grain that had been cut and the grain that was still growing. It burned their vineyards and olive trees too.

decisions.choice: stacked sheaves and standing grain: the harvest both cut and uncut
decisions.reason: In the wheat harvest (verse 1) some fields were already cut and the sheaves piled in stacks to dry, while others still stood. The fire took both, so a whole year's bread was lost.

decisions.choice: vineyard, olive: the vineyards and the olive groves
decisions.reason: The Hebrew sets "vineyard" and "olive" side by side without "and". It may mean olive orchards alone, but the list builds up from grain to vines to olives, the three main crops of the land (Deuteronomy 7:13), so the loss reached every kind of produce.

decisions.choice: let the foxes loose / let the foxes run
decisions.reason: The Hebrew says only "he sent"; Balanced and Readable name the foxes so the sentence is clear.

records.source: וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ פְלִשְׁתִּים֮ מִ֣י עָ֣שָׂה זֹאת֒ וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ שִׁמְשׁוֹן֙ חֲתַ֣ן הַתִּמְנִ֔י כִּ֚י לָקַ֣ח אֶת־אִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וַֽיִּתְּנָ֖הּ לְמֵרֵעֵ֑הוּ וַיַּעֲל֣וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַיִּשְׂרְפ֥וּ אוֹתָ֛הּ וְאֶת־אָבִ֖יהָ בָּאֵֽשׁ׃
records.gloss: And said [the] Philistines, who did this? And they said, Samson, [the] son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to his companion. And went up [the] Philistines and burned her and her father with fire.
pieces: The Philistines asked, "Who did this?" They were told, "Samson, the Timnite's son-in-law, because the man took his wife and gave her to his companion." So the Philistines went up and burned her to death, and her father with her.

L.6: And the Philistines said, "Who did this?" And they said, "Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to his companion." And the Philistines went up and burned her and her father with fire.

R.6: The Philistines asked, "Who did this?" Someone answered, "Samson did it. He married the daughter of a man from Timnah, but her father gave her to Samson's friend." So the Philistines went up to Timnah and burned the woman and her father to death.

decisions.choice: the Timnite: the man of Timnah, Samson's father-in-law
decisions.reason: Timnah was the Philistine town where Samson found his wife (14:1). The Philistines blame the father-in-law as the cause of Samson's revenge.

decisions.choice: burned her and her father with fire: the threat of 14:15 carried out
decisions.reason: At the feast the Philistine guests had threatened to burn the woman and her father's house if she did not get the riddle's answer for them (14:15). She did what they asked, and the same fate came on her anyway. The violence on each side keeps growing.

decisions.choice: her father: the Hebrew text
decisions.reason: Many manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation read "her and her father's house", which matches the threat of 14:15. The Hebrew text, "her father", is kept; the sense is close either way.

decisions.choice: They were told / Someone answered; burned ... to death
decisions.reason: "They said" has no named subject; Balanced and Readable make it an answer given to the Philistines. Readable explains who the Timnite was and leaves the matter of who "took" the wife to the father, as the Hebrew means.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָהֶם֙ שִׁמְשׁ֔וֹן אִֽם־תַּעֲשׂ֖וּן כָּזֹ֑את כִּ֛י אִם־נִקַּ֥מְתִּי בָכֶ֖ם וְאַחַ֥ר אֶחְדָּֽל׃
records.gloss: And said to them Samson, if you do like this, surely if I have avenged myself on you, and after I will stop.
pieces: Samson said to them, "Since you have acted like this, I swear I will take revenge on you, and only after that will I stop."

L.7: And Samson said to them, "If you do like this, surely I will take vengeance on you, and after [that] I will stop."

R.7: Samson told them, "Because you did this, I will get even with you. I will not stop until I do."

decisions.choice: if ... surely if I have taken vengeance ... and after I will stop: an oath that he will not rest until he has paid them back
decisions.reason: "If you do like this" refers to what they have just done, not to a future act. The words "surely if" are the form of a vow: Samson swears that he will have his revenge first, and only then stop.

decisions.choice: taken vengeance: paid back a wrong
decisions.reason: The verb means to avenge a wrong done to oneself or one's family. Samson acts for his own wrong, though in doing so he also strikes the people who rule Israel (13:5; 14:4).

decisions.choice: Since you have acted like this, I swear ... / Because you did this ... I will not stop until I do
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable make clear that "if" points to what the Philistines have already done, and give the oath in plain words.

records.source: וַיַּ֨ךְ אוֹתָ֥ם שׁ֛וֹק עַל־יָרֵ֖ךְ מַכָּ֣ה גְדוֹלָ֑ה וַיֵּ֣רֶד וַיֵּ֔שֶׁב בִּסְעִ֖יף סֶ֥לַע עֵיטָֽם׃ס
records.gloss: And he struck them leg on thigh, a slaughter great; and he went down and dwelt in [the] cleft of [the] rock of Etam.
pieces: He struck them down hip and thigh, a great slaughter. Then he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.

L.8: And he struck them leg on thigh, a great slaughter. And he went down and stayed in the cleft of the rock of Etam.

R.8: He attacked them without mercy and killed many of them. Then he went down and stayed in a cave in the rock of Etam.

decisions.choice: leg on thigh: a crushing, merciless attack
decisions.reason: The phrase pictures bodies cut down and piled up, limbs on limbs. It is not found elsewhere in the Bible, but the words that follow, "a great slaughter", show its sense: a complete defeat.

decisions.choice: the cleft of the rock of Etam: a hiding place in a cliff in Judah
decisions.reason: Etam was in the hill country of Judah, near Bethlehem (2 Chronicles 11:6). A "cleft" is a split or opening in the rock, a place hard to reach where a man could hide and defend himself. Samson "went down" to it, and the men of Judah later bring him "up" from it (verse 13).

decisions.choice: hip and thigh
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the picture in a form English can follow; Readable gives its meaning instead.

decisions.choice: a cave in the rock
decisions.reason: Readable says "cave" for "cleft", an opening in the rock big enough to stay in.

records.source: וַיַּעֲל֣וּ פְלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וַֽיַּחֲנ֖וּ בִּיהוּדָ֑ה וַיִּנָּטְשׁ֖וּ בַּלֶּֽחִי׃
records.gloss: And went up [the] Philistines and camped in Judah, and spread out in Lehi.
pieces: Then the Philistines went up, camped in Judah, and spread out around Lehi.

L.9: And the Philistines went up and camped in Judah, and spread out at Lehi.

R.9: Then the Philistines came up into Judah. They set up camp and spread out near a place called Lehi.

decisions.choice: Lehi: a place in Judah whose name means "jawbone"
decisions.reason: The name sounds like the word for "jawbone" that the story turns on (verses 15-17). Its site is not known for certain. The narrator may use the name it was known by later, after these events (verse 17).

decisions.choice: spread out: deployed in raiding parties
decisions.reason: The verb is used of troops spreading out over an area to raid it (1 Samuel 30:16; 2 Samuel 5:18). The Philistines came in force, ready to plunder Judah unless Samson was given up.

records.heading: The jawbone of a donkey

records.source: וַיֹּֽאמְרוּ֙ אִ֣ישׁ יְהוּדָ֔ה לָמָ֖ה עֲלִיתֶ֣ם עָלֵ֑ינוּ וַיֹּאמְר֗וּ לֶאֱס֤וֹר אֶת־שִׁמְשׁוֹן֙ עָלִ֔ינוּ לַעֲשׂ֣וֹת ל֔וֹ כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר עָ֥שָׂה לָֽנוּ׃
records.gloss: And said [the] men of Judah, why have you come up against us? And they said, to bind Samson we have come up, to do to him as he did to us.
pieces: The men of Judah asked, "Why have you come to attack us?" They answered, "We have come to take Samson prisoner, to do to him what he did to us."

L.10: And the men of Judah said, "Why have you come up against us?" And they said, "We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us."

R.10: The men of Judah asked, "Why have you come to fight us?" The Philistines answered, "We came to capture Samson. We will do to him what he did to us."

decisions.choice: bind: tie up as a prisoner
decisions.reason: To bind someone is to take him captive. The word comes back through the story: the men of Judah bind Samson (verses 12-13), and the ropes fall from his hands (verse 14).

decisions.choice: to do to him as he did to us: the rule of revenge for revenge
decisions.reason: The Philistines speak the same way as Samson (verse 11): each side says it is only paying back what was done to it. The words echo the law of like for like (Leviticus 24:19), turned into a reason for endless revenge.

decisions.choice: take Samson prisoner / capture Samson
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "bind" means here; Literal keeps the word, which the story repeats.

records.source: וַיֵּרְד֡וּ שְׁלֹשֶׁת֩ אֲלָפִ֨ים אִ֜ישׁ מִֽיהוּדָ֗ה אֶל־סְעִיף֮ סֶ֣לַע עֵיטָם֒ וַיֹּאמְר֣וּ לְשִׁמְשׁ֗וֹן הֲלֹ֤א יָדַ֨עְתָּ֙ כִּֽי־מֹשְׁלִ֥ים בָּ֨נוּ֙ פְּלִשְׁתִּ֔ים וּמַה־זֹּ֖את עָשִׂ֣יתָ לָּ֑נוּ וַיֹּ֣אמֶר לָהֶ֔ם כַּאֲשֶׁר֙ עָ֣שׂוּ לִ֔י כֵּ֖ן עָשִׂ֥יתִי לָהֶֽם׃
records.gloss: And went down three thousand men of Judah to [the] cleft of [the] rock of Etam, and they said to Samson, [do] not you know that [are] ruling over us [the] Philistines? and what [is] this you have done to us? And he said to them, as they did to me, so I have done to them.
pieces: Then 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft in the rock of Etam and said to Samson, "Do you not know that we are ruled by the Philistines? What is this you have brought on us?" He answered them, "I only did to them what they did to me."

L.11: And 3,000 men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam, and they said to Samson, "Do you not know that the Philistines [are] ruling over us? And what [is] this you have done to us?" And he said to them, "As they did to me, so I have done to them."

R.11: So 3,000 men from Judah went down to the cave in the rock of Etam. They said to Samson, "The Philistines are our rulers. Surely you know that! Look at the trouble you have brought on us!" Samson answered, "They did this to me first, so I did the same to them."

decisions.choice: the Philistines rule over us: Judah accepts Philistine rule
decisions.reason: Judah had led the tribes into battle at the start of the book (1:1-2), but now it sends three thousand men, not to fight the Philistines, but to hand over the one man fighting them. The Philistines' rule over Israel was the setting of Samson's whole story (13:1; 14:4).

decisions.choice: three thousand: a large band
decisions.reason: "Thousand" is kept, as in the census of Numbers 1 (see the note there on the size of the unit). The point is the contrast: thousands come out against one man of their own people.

decisions.choice: as they did to me, so I have done to them: Samson's answer in the Philistines' own words
decisions.reason: Samson uses the same words as the Philistines in verse 10, "to do as he did to us". Each side claims only to be paying back what it received.

decisions.choice: The Philistines are our rulers. Surely you know that! Look at the trouble ...
decisions.reason: Readable turns the two questions into the statements they imply: the men of Judah are not asking for information but rebuking Samson.

records.source: וַיֹּ֤אמְרוּ לוֹ֙ לֶאֱסָרְךָ֣ יָרַ֔דְנוּ לְתִתְּךָ֖ בְּיַד־פְּלִשְׁתִּ֑ים וַיֹּ֤אמֶר לָהֶם֙ שִׁמְשׁ֔וֹן הִשָּׁבְע֣וּ לִ֔י פֶּֽן־תִּפְגְּע֥וּן בִּ֖י אַתֶּֽם׃
records.gloss: And they said to him, to bind you we have come down, to give you into [the] hand of [the] Philistines. And said to them Samson, swear to me lest fall on me you.
pieces: They told him, "We have come down to tie you up and hand you over to the Philistines." Then Samson said, "Give me your oath that you yourselves will not attack me."

L.12: And they said to him, "We have come down to bind you, to give you into the hand of the Philistines." And Samson said to them, "Swear to me that you yourselves will not fall on me."

R.12: They told him, "We have come to tie you up and give you to the Philistines." Samson said, "Promise me with an oath that you will not kill me yourselves."

decisions.choice: fall on me: attack me, kill me
decisions.reason: The verb means to meet or strike someone, and often to strike him down (Judges 8:21; 1 Samuel 22:17-18). Samson will let his own people bind him, but not harm him; "you yourselves" is emphatic.

decisions.choice: give you into the hand of the Philistines: hand you over to their power
decisions.reason: "Hand" stands for power or control, as in the phrase used when God gives a people into an enemy's hand (2:14; 13:1).

decisions.choice: tie you up and hand you over / give you to
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "tie up" for "bind", and "hand over" for "give into the hand of".

records.source: וַיֹּ֧אמְרוּ ל֣וֹ לֵאמֹ֗ר לֹ֚אכִּֽי־אָסֹ֤ר נֶֽאֱסָרְךָ֙ וּנְתַנּ֣וּךָ בְיָדָ֔ם וְהָמֵ֖ת לֹ֣א נְמִיתֶ֑ךָ וַיַּאַסְרֻ֗הוּ בִּשְׁנַ֨יִם֙ עֲבֹתִ֣ים חֲדָשִׁ֔ים וַֽיַּעֲל֖וּהוּ מִן־הַסָּֽלַע׃
records.gloss: And they said to him, saying, no; but binding we will bind you and give you into their hand, but killing not we will kill you. And they bound him with two ropes new and brought him up from the rock.
pieces: "No," they told him, "we will only tie you up and hand you over to them. We will certainly not kill you." So they tied him with two new ropes and took him up out of the cleft in the rock.

L.13: And they said to him, "No; but we will surely bind you and give you into their hand, but we will surely not kill you." And they bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.

R.13: "We will not kill you," they promised. "We will only tie you up and give you to the Philistines." So they tied him up with two new ropes and led him up out of the cave in the rock.

decisions.choice: binding we will bind ... killing we will not kill: firm promises
decisions.reason: Both verbs are doubled for emphasis. The men of Judah promise that they will do no more than bind him, and that they will certainly not put him to death.

decisions.choice: two new ropes: strong ropes, never weakened by use
decisions.reason: New ropes were the strongest kind, and two of them made sure he could not break loose. Delilah later tries new ropes too (16:11-12).

decisions.choice: "We will not kill you" first
decisions.reason: Readable puts the promise not to kill him first, since that answers what Samson asked them to swear.

records.source: הוּא־בָ֣א עַד־לֶ֔חִי וּפִלְשִׁתִּ֖יםהֵרִ֣יעוּ לִקְרָאת֑וֹ וַתִּצְלַ֨ח עָלָ֜יו ר֣וּחַ יְהוָ֗ה וַתִּהְיֶ֨ינָה הָעֲבֹתִ֜ים אֲשֶׁ֣ר עַל־זְרוֹעוֹתָ֗יו כַּפִּשְׁתִּים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בָּעֲר֣וּ בָאֵ֔שׁ וַיִּמַּ֥סּוּ אֱסוּרָ֖יו מֵעַ֥ל יָדָֽיו׃
records.gloss: He [was] coming to Lehi, and [the] Philistines shouted to meet him; and rushed on him [the] Spirit of Yahweh, and became the ropes which [were] on his arms like flax which they burned with fire, and melted his bonds from on his hands.
pieces: As he came to Lehi, the Philistines ran shouting to meet him. Then the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on him. The ropes on his arms became like flax caught in a fire, and his bonds melted away from his hands.

L.14: He was coming to Lehi, and the Philistines shouted [as they came] to meet him. And the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on him, and the ropes that [were] on his arms became like flax that has burned with fire, and his bonds melted from off his hands.

R.14: When Samson came to Lehi, the Philistines ran toward him, shouting in triumph. Then the Spirit of {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} rushed on him. The ropes on his arms became as weak as burned threads, and they fell off his hands.

decisions.choice: shouted: a battle cry or shout of triumph
decisions.reason: The verb is used of the shout raised in battle or in victory (Joshua 6:5; 1 Samuel 17:20). The Philistines shout because their enemy is being handed over to them bound.

decisions.choice: the Spirit of the LORD rushed on him: God's power came on him suddenly
decisions.reason: The same verb is used when the Spirit came on Samson to kill the lion (14:6) and the men of Ashkelon (14:19). His strength is shown to be God's gift, not his own.

decisions.choice: like flax burned with fire: as weak as charred threads
decisions.reason: Flax was the plant from which linen thread was made. Thread that has been in a fire falls apart at a touch, and the new ropes became just as weak. The fire also recalls the burning in verses 5-6.

decisions.choice: rushed on him
decisions.reason: Every level keeps "rushed on", as in 14:6 and 14:19, a plain picture of the Spirit coming with sudden power.

records.source: וַיִּמְצָ֥א לְחִֽי־חֲמ֖וֹר טְרִיָּ֑ה וַיִּשְׁלַ֤ח יָדוֹ֙ וַיִּקָּחֶ֔הָ וַיַּךְ־בָּ֖הּ אֶ֥לֶף אִֽישׁ׃
records.gloss: And he found a jawbone of a donkey, fresh, and he stretched out his hand and took it, and struck down with it a thousand men.
pieces: He came upon the fresh jawbone of a donkey. He reached out and took hold of it, and with it he struck down 1,000 men.

L.15: And he found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, and he stretched out his hand and took it, and struck down 1,000 men with it.

R.15: Samson saw the jawbone of a donkey that had not been dead long. He reached down and picked it up, and he killed 1,000 men with it.

decisions.choice: fresh: from an animal recently dead
decisions.reason: A fresh jawbone was still heavy and tough, not dry and brittle, so it could serve as a club. It also came from a dead body, something a Nazirite was to keep away from (Numbers 6:6; Judges 13:5), as with the lion in 14:8-9.

decisions.choice: a thousand men: a very large number killed
decisions.reason: "Thousand" is kept, as in verse 11. Samson repeats the number in his saying (verse 16).

decisions.choice: that had not been dead long
decisions.reason: Readable explains "fresh", which could otherwise suggest a jawbone that was clean or new.

records.source: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר שִׁמְשׁ֔וֹן בִּלְחִ֣י הַחֲמ֔וֹר חֲמ֖וֹר חֲמֹרָתָ֑יִם בִּלְחִ֣י הַחֲמ֔וֹר הִכֵּ֖יתִי אֶ֥לֶף אִֽישׁ׃
records.gloss: And said Samson, with [the] jawbone of the donkey, a heap, two heaps; with [the] jawbone of the donkey I struck down a thousand men.
pieces: Then Samson said, \q "With a donkey's jawbone, a heap, two heaps of them; \q with a donkey's jawbone I struck down a thousand men!"

L.16: And Samson said, \q "With the jawbone of the donkey, a heap, two heaps; \q with the jawbone of the donkey I struck down a thousand men."

R.16: Then Samson said, \q "With a donkey's jawbone I piled them up in heaps. \q With a donkey's jawbone I killed a thousand men!"

decisions.choice: donkey ... a heap, two heaps: a play on two words that sound the same
decisions.reason: The Hebrew word for "donkey" and the word for "heap" are spelled with the same letters and sound almost alike, so the saying rings with the same sound four times in a row. Samson boasts that one donkey's jawbone left the bodies of his enemies lying in heaps. The play on words cannot be carried over into another language, so the meaning is kept and this note explains the sound.

decisions.choice: a heap, two heaps: piles of the dead
alternatives: I have made donkeys of them
I have utterly wiped them out
decisions.reason: The two words are the noun "heap" and its form for "two heaps", meaning heaps upon heaps. The letters can also be read as a verb, giving "I have made donkeys of them" or "I have reddened them" (with blood), and the ancient Greek translation reads "I have utterly wiped them out". The reading of the Hebrew vowels, "a heap, two heaps", is kept.

decisions.choice: Samson's saying: a short victory song
decisions.reason: Like his riddle at the feast (14:14, 18), Samson's boast is set in two balanced lines, the second repeating the first and completing it. It is the kind of short song sung over a victory (compare 1 Samuel 18:7).

decisions.choice: a heap, two heaps of them / piled them up in heaps
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the short, broken phrase of the saying and adds "of them" so it is clear the heaps are the dead. Readable says it in a full sentence. No level tries to imitate the sound play with a pun of its own, since an English pun would change the words.

records.source: וַֽיְהִי֙ כְּכַלֹּת֣וֹ לְדַבֵּ֔ר וַיַּשְׁלֵ֥ךְ הַלְּחִ֖י מִיָּד֑וֹ וַיִּקְרָ֛א לַמָּק֥וֹם הַה֖וּא רָ֥מַת לֶֽחִי׃
records.gloss: And it was when he finished to speak, and he threw the jawbone from his hand, and he called the place that Ramath-lehi.
pieces: When he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone away, and that place was called Ramath-lehi.

L.17: And it was, when he had finished speaking, he threw the jawbone from his hand, and he called that place Ramath-lehi.

R.17: When Samson finished speaking, he threw the jawbone away. He named that place Ramath-lehi, which means "Jawbone Hill."

decisions.choice: Ramath-lehi: "the height of the jawbone"
decisions.reason: The name means "height" or "hill of the jawbone". It also sounds like a word meaning "throwing", so it may recall how Samson threw the jawbone away there. The name explains why the place was called Lehi (verse 9).

decisions.choice: he called: Samson named the place
decisions.reason: The subject is Samson; he names the place after what he did there, as in verse 19.

decisions.choice: that place was called
decisions.reason: Balanced turns "he called" around to keep the focus on the name; it is still Samson who gives it.

decisions.choice: which means "Jawbone Hill"
decisions.reason: Readable explains the name, since the story's point is lost without it.

records.source: וַיִּצְמָא֮ מְאֹד֒ וַיִּקְרָ֤א אֶל־יְהוָה֙ וַיֹּאמַ֔ר אַתָּה֙ נָתַ֣תָּ בְיַֽד־עַבְדְּךָ֔ אֶת־הַתְּשׁוּעָ֥ה הַגְּדֹלָ֖ה הַזֹּ֑את וְעַתָּה֙ אָמ֣וּת בַּצָּמָ֔א וְנָפַלְתִּ֖י בְּיַ֥ד הָעֲרֵלִֽים׃
records.gloss: And he was thirsty very, and he called to Yahweh and said, you have given by [the] hand of your servant the deliverance the great the this, and now I will die by thirst and fall into [the] hand of the uncircumcised.
pieces: He was very thirsty, and he called out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "You have given this great victory by the hand of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant. Now must I die of thirst and fall into the power of these uncircumcised men?"

L.18: And he was very thirsty, and he called to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}} and said, "You have given this great deliverance by the hand of {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} slave, and now shall I die of thirst and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised?"

R.18: Samson was very thirsty, so he cried out to {{divine_name:the LORD|Yahweh}}, "You used me, {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} servant, to win this great victory. Am I now going to die of thirst? Will these Philistines, who are not circumcised, get hold of me after all?"

decisions.choice: deliverance: a rescue or victory that God gives
decisions.reason: The word means rescue, help or victory, and Samson gives the credit to God: "You have given" it. It is the first time in his story that he speaks to God.

decisions.choice: and now I will die ...: a complaint put as a question
decisions.reason: The Hebrew has no question word, but the sense is a protest: after such a victory, is God going to let him die of thirst? Many Hebrew questions are marked only by the tone of the words.

decisions.choice: the uncircumcised: the Philistines
decisions.reason: The Philistines were known in Israel as a people who did not practice circumcision, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17:10-11). Samson's parents use the same word of them (14:3).

decisions.choice: slave (Literal), servant (Balanced and Readable)
decisions.reason: Samson calls himself the LORD's servant, a humble way of speaking of oneself before a master. As elsewhere, Literal keeps "slave" and Balanced and Readable say "servant".

decisions.choice: You used me ... to win; these Philistines, who are not circumcised
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly that Samson means himself, and names the Philistines, explaining what "uncircumcised" refers to.

records.source: וַיִּבְקַ֨ע אֱלֹהִ֜ים אֶת־הַמַּכְתֵּ֣שׁ אֲשֶׁר־בַּלֶּ֗חִי וַיֵּצְא֨וּ מִמֶּ֤נּוּ מַ֨יִם֙ וַיֵּ֔שְׁתְּ וַתָּ֥שָׁב רוּח֖וֹ וַיֶּ֑חִי עַל־כֵּ֣ן׀קָרָ֣א שְׁמָ֗הּ עֵ֤ין הַקּוֹרֵא֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר בַּלֶּ֔חִי עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה׃
records.gloss: And split God the hollow which [is] in Lehi, and came out from it water, and he drank, and returned his spirit and he revived; therefore he called its name En-hakkore, which [is] in Lehi until the day the this.
pieces: So God split open the hollow at Lehi, and water flowed from it. Samson drank, his strength came back, and he revived. That is why he named it En-hakkore. It is still there at Lehi to this day.

L.19: And God split open the hollow place that [is] at Lehi, and water came out of it, and he drank, and his spirit returned, and he revived. Therefore he called its name En-hakkore; it [is] at Lehi to this day.

R.19: Then God split open a hollow in the ground at Lehi, and water flowed out of it. Samson drank, and his strength came back. He felt alive again. So he named the spring En-hakkore, which means "Spring of the One Who Called." It is still at Lehi today.

decisions.choice: the hollow place at Lehi: a basin-shaped hollow in the ground
decisions.reason: The word means a mortar, the bowl in which grain was pounded, and so a hollow shaped like one. "Lehi" here is the place, as at the end of the verse, not the jawbone that Samson had already thrown away (verse 17), though the Hebrew words could be read "in the jawbone".

decisions.choice: his spirit returned and he revived: his strength came back
decisions.reason: "Spirit" here is Samson's own breath and life force, worn out with thirst, not the Spirit of the LORD. The same words are used when Jacob's spirit revived at the news about Joseph (Genesis 45:27).

decisions.choice: En-hakkore: "the spring of the one who called"
decisions.reason: The name means "spring of the caller". It recalls how Samson "called" to the LORD (verse 18), using the same verb. The same word can also mean a partridge (1 Samuel 26:20), a bird named for its call, which may have been an older sense of the name.

decisions.choice: to this day: still known when the book was written
decisions.reason: The phrase tells the reader that the spring could still be seen at the time the story was written down, as with other places in Judges (1:26; 6:24).

decisions.choice: strength
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say "strength" for "spirit", so that it is not taken for the Spirit of God.

decisions.choice: the spring ... which means "Spring of the One Who Called"
decisions.reason: Readable explains the name and says that "it" is the spring.

records.source: וַיִּשְׁפֹּ֧ט אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵ֛ל בִּימֵ֥י פְלִשְׁתִּ֖ים עֶשְׂרִ֥ים שָׁנָֽה׃פ
records.gloss: And he judged Israel in [the] days of [the] Philistines twenty years.
pieces: In the days of the Philistines, Samson judged Israel for twenty years.

L.20: And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.

R.20: Samson led Israel for twenty years during the time when the Philistines ruled the land.

decisions.choice: judged Israel: led and governed Israel
decisions.reason: As at 2:16, a judge was a leader raised up to rescue Israel and govern it, more than a judge in a court.

decisions.choice: in the days of the Philistines: while the Philistines still ruled
decisions.reason: The Philistines ruled Israel for forty years (13:1), and Samson was only to begin Israel's rescue from them (13:5). His twenty years fall within that time; the Philistines were not driven out until later (1 Samuel 7:13). The same twenty years are given again at his death (16:31).

decisions.choice: led; when the Philistines ruled the land
decisions.reason: Readable says "led" for "judged", as at 2:16, and spells out what "the days of the Philistines" means.
